Amazon Bestselling Books
Price vs. User Rating Trend Analysis (2009–2019)

A comprehensive analysis of how book pricing strategies relate to customer satisfaction across Fiction and Non-Fiction genres over a decade of Amazon bestseller data.

Dataset: 550 records Timeframe: 2009–2019 Prepared: May 2026

Figure 1: Genre split across all 550 bestseller records. Non-Fiction dominates at 56.4%.

The dataset spans 2009–2019 (550 records) with 351 unique titles from 248 authors. The average book has a user rating of 4.62/5.0 and is priced at $13.10 (median: $11.00).

Non-Fiction accounts for 56.4% of bestseller appearances (310 records) compared to Fiction at 43.6% (240 records). This 56/44 split reflects non-fiction's broader appeal across self-help, biography, reference, and children's categories.

Ratings are concentrated in the 4.3–4.9 range (μ=4.62, σ=0.227), consistent with the survivorship bias inherent in bestseller data — these are already market-validated titles.

Price range: $0 – $105 Rating std. dev: 0.227 Median price: $11.00

2. Price vs. User Rating: Correlation Analysis

Quantify and visualize the relationship between book price and user rating. Determine whether higher prices are associated with higher or lower ratings.

Figure 2: Scatter plot of Price vs. User Rating for all 550 records, with linear trend line and Pearson correlation coefficient.
r = -0.1331  |  p = 0.0018
Overall Pearson Correlation

The Pearson correlation coefficient between price and user rating is r = -0.1331 (p = 0.0018), indicating a weak negative (statistically significant, p=0.0018) correlation.

In practical terms: higher prices do not translate to higher customer satisfaction. If anything, there is a slight tendency for more expensive books to receive marginally lower ratings. This challenges the assumption that price signals quality in the book market.

Key Finding: The negative correlation, while weak (|r| < 0.15), is statistically significant for the overall dataset and for Non-Fiction. For Fiction, the correlation is not significant — suggesting that Fiction readers are less price-sensitive in their rating behavior. The data does not support a "you get what you pay for" narrative in bestselling books.

Compare average price, user rating, and review counts between genres. Highlight key differences and identify which genre delivers better perceived value.

4. Year-over-Year Trends in Pricing and Ratings

Analyze how average book prices, user ratings, and review volumes have changed annually from 2009 to 2019. Identify inflection points and notable shifts.

Figure 6: Annual trends in average price, user rating, review count, and genre composition (2009–2019).
Figure 7: Annual rating range (min–max band) with mean trend line, showing tightening and widening of quality dispersion over time.

Pricing Trends

Average bestseller prices fluctuated between $10.08 (2019) and $15.40 (2009). The most dramatic shift was the -4.22 USD drop from 2014→2015, followed by a recovery with the largest single-year increase of +$2.76 from 2015→2016.

Fiction pricing has been notably more stable, ranging from $8.76 (2018) to $15.58 (2009). Non-Fiction shows more volatility, with prices swinging between $10.57 and $20.81 — driven by premium reference works and higher-priced non-fiction categories.

Rating Trends

Average ratings show a gradual upward trajectory from 4.532 (2012) to a peak of 4.740 (2019). This may reflect improving book quality, more generous rating behavior over time, or algorithmic curation by Amazon surfacing higher-rated titles to bestseller status.

Notably, the largest year-over-year rating improvement was +0.072 (2018→2019), while the largest decline was -0.026 (2009→2010) — changes that are meaningful in the context of the narrow 4.3–4.9 rating band.

Genre Composition Shifts

The Fiction/Non-Fiction balance has not been static. Non-Fiction's share of the bestseller list expanded significantly in the early-to-mid 2010s, coinciding with the adult coloring book trend and a wave of political memoirs. Fiction maintained a more consistent presence throughout the decade.

Figure 8: Books per price segment and average rating within each segment. The $$0–$5 segment has the highest average rating at 4.711.

Jeff Kinney (Diary of a Wimpy Kid series) leads with 12 appearances — appearing every year — maintaining a remarkable 4.80 average rating at just $9.25 average price. His formula of affordable pricing and consistent quality demonstrates that moderate pricing paired with strong reader loyalty is a reliable path to sustained bestseller status.

Gary Chapman (The 5 Love Languages) and Suzanne Collins (The Hunger Games) each appear 11 times, representing Non-Fiction and Fiction respectively. Chapman commands a 86% higher average price ($17.18 vs $9.25) than Kinney with slightly lower ratings.

Pattern: Authors with the highest average ratings (Eric Carle: 4.90, Dav Pilkey: 4.90, Sarah Young: 4.90) all price their books below the market average ($5.00–$8.00). No author with an average price above $20 achieved a rating above 4.70, reinforcing the finding that price and satisfaction are not positively linked in this market.

6. Strategic Recommendations

Synthesize findings into actionable pricing and positioning recommendations for publishers and retailers targeting the Amazon bestseller list.

Recommendation 01
Resist Premium-Price Positioning for Ratings
The data shows a weak but statistically significant negative correlation (r = -0.1331) between price and rating. Higher-priced books do not earn higher ratings. Publishers should not assume that premium pricing will be validated by customer satisfaction — the opposite is more likely.
← Section 2: Correlation Analysis
Recommendation 02
Price Fiction Competitively — Optimize for Volume
Fiction achieves 4.65 average rating at $10.85 — outperforming Non-Fiction on both satisfaction and engagement per dollar. Fiction buyers are review-active (15,684 avg reviews vs. 9,065 for Non-Fiction). Competitive pricing amplifies discovery through review velocity.
← Section 3: Genre Comparison
Recommendation 03
Leverage the $0–$10 Sweet Spot for Maximum Ratings
Books priced under $10 consistently achieve the highest average ratings. The $0–$5 segment had the highest rating average. Free/promotional pricing (12 books at $0) averaged 4.77 — above the 4.62 overall mean — suggesting promotional pricing can boost satisfaction signals without harming perceived quality.
← Section 4: Price Segment Analysis
Recommendation 04
Justify Non-Fiction Premiums with Perceived Authority
Non-Fiction prices average 37% higher ($14.84 vs. $10.85) but generate lower ratings (4.60 vs. 4.65). This premium can only be sustained if the content delivers clear, differentiated value. Publishers should ensure premium Non-Fiction pricing is backed by author credentials, original research, or proprietary frameworks.
← Sections 3 & 5: Genre and Author Analysis
Recommendation 05
Monitor the 2014–2016 Pricing Inflection Point
The -$4.22 price drop (2014→2015) followed by +$2.76 recovery (2015→2016) represents the most volatile pricing period in the dataset. This coincides with the adult coloring book boom and may reflect market correction. Similar dislocations are forecast opportunities — be ready to adjust pricing strategy during category fads.
← Section 4: Temporal Trends
Recommendation 06
Build Author Franchises at Accessible Price Points
The top 3 most-appearing authors (Jeff Kinney, Rick Riordan, Gary Chapman) average 11+ appearances each with $9–$17 price ranges and 4.73+ ratings. Consistency and series-building at moderate price points drive repeat bestseller appearances more reliably than one-off premium titles.
← Section 5: Top Authors

Methodology & Data Notes

Data Source: Kaggle dataset "Amazon Bestsellers: Price vs User Rating Analysis" — 550 records representing the top 50 bestselling books on Amazon for each year from 2009 to 2019.

Statistical Methods: Pearson correlation coefficient (r) with two-tailed p-value for price–rating relationships. Year-over-year changes computed as arithmetic differences in annual means. Price segments defined as $0–$5, $6–$10, $11–$15, $16–$20, and $21+.

Limitations: (1) The dataset captures only the top 50 per year — findings apply to bestsellers, not the broader book market. (2) Causality cannot be inferred from correlation; price may correlate with unobserved variables (genre conventions, publisher size, marketing spend) that influence ratings. (3) Rating distributions are compressed (4.3–4.9), limiting the magnitude of observable correlations. (4) Duplicate entries exist by design — the same book can appear in multiple years.
